flawed_step: Step 4: concluding a·p + (1-a)·q > b·r + (1-b)·s from p>r and q>s. This only follows when a=b. Here a=P(C|T) and b=P(C|not-T), which need not be equal (Simpson's paradox).
counterexample: Use 700 equally likely individuals (the kidney-stone data). T and C (87 people): 81 successes. T and not-C (263): 192 successes. not-T and C (270): 234 successes. not-T and not-C (80): 55 successes. Within strata: 81/87 ≈ 0.931 > 234/270 ≈ 0.867, and 192/263 ≈ 0.730 > 55/80 = 0.6875. Overall: P(S|T) = 273/350 = 0.78 < P(S|not-T) = 289/350 ≈ 0.826. All four cells have positive probability.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Law of total probability: P(S|T) = P(S|T,C)·P(C|T) + P(S|T,¬C)·P(¬C|T). JUSTIFIED: all the conditionals are defined by the positivity assumptions.
2. Likewise, P(S|¬T) = P(S|¬T,C)·P(C|¬T) + P(S|¬T,¬C)·P(¬C|¬T). JUSTIFIED, same reason.
3. Write p=P(S|T,C), q=P(S|T,¬C), r=P(S|¬T,C), s=P(S|¬T,¬C), a=P(C|T), b=P(C|¬T). The hypotheses give p>r and q>s. JUSTIFIED: this is just the hypothesis.
4. So a·p+(1-a)·q > b·r+(1-b)·s. NOT JUSTIFIED: the two sides are averages with different weights. If a=b the claim holds, but a≠b in general. For example, when p>q, putting a large weight b on r and a small weight a on p can reverse the order.
5. Therefore P(S|T) > P(S|¬T). NOT JUSTIFIED: it depends on step 4.
Counterexample check (finite uniform space with 700 points): p=81/87≈0.931 > r=234/270≈0.867, and q=192/263≈0.730 > s=55/80=0.6875. But a=87/350 and b=270/350 differ a lot, so P(S|T)=273/350=0.78 < P(S|¬T)=289/350≈0.826. The hypotheses hold and the conclusion fails, so the statement is false.
